source.name: sp_DynamicSearch

assumptions: The procedure is intended to return a result set, so it's converted to a FUNCTION returning TABLE
NVARCHAR mapped to VARCHAR (PostgreSQL uses UTF-8 by default)
QUOTENAME() mapped to format() with %I identifier placeholder for SQL injection protection
The calling application can handle the change from PROCEDURE to FUNCTION
The table structure is unknown, so RETURNS TABLE without explicit column definitions is used
Schema 'dbo' exists in PostgreSQL or will be created separately

reviewFlags.reason: PostgreSQL requires explicit column definitions in RETURNS TABLE for strongly-typed returns, or use RETURNS SETOF RECORD. The current implementation returns an anonymous record set which may require the caller to use column definition lists in the query.

Dynamic SQL with user-supplied table and column names poses SQL injection risks. Verify that input validation/sanitization exists at the application layer. The format() function with %I provides identifier quoting but doesn't validate table/column existence.
SQL Server procedure converted to PostgreSQL function because it returns a result set. Calling syntax changes from EXEC to SELECT * FROM function_name(). Verify all calling code is updated.
No explicit error handling added. Consider adding EXCEPTION block to handle cases where table or column doesn't exist, or when data type mismatches occur.

compatibilityNotes.description: SQL Server procedures can return result sets directly. PostgreSQL requires functions with RETURNS TABLE/SETOF. Callers must use SELECT * FROM function_name() instead of EXEC procedure_name.
PostgreSQL's format() function with %I is used instead of QUOTENAME(). Both provide identifier quoting but syntax differs. EXECUTE...USING replaces sp_executesql.
SET NOCOUNT ON has no direct equivalent in PostgreSQL and is omitted. PostgreSQL functions don't send row count messages by default.
The 'dbo' schema is preserved but must exist in PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL's default schema is 'public'. Consider schema search_path configuration.
Without knowing the target table structure, the function returns an untyped record set. Callers may need to provide column definitions: SELECT * FROM function_name() AS t(col1 type1, col2 type2, ...)
